description: nf-core/pangenome context, aligned to the pinned 1.1.3 schema. One pangenome variation graph from ONE combined, bgzipped multi-genome FASTA (an A.ASM sample); the pipeline reads no samplesheet.

n_haplotypes.help: Required, no upstream default: the number of haplotypes in the combined FASTA, which is the number of distinct PanSN sample#haplotype prefixes in its sequence names (a haploid genome is one; a phased diploid assembly is two). Set from the A.ASM sample's GenomeCount by the parameter atlas, and asked for when that is not recorded. A wrong count does not error: smoothxg and wfmash scale their work by it.

wfmash_map_pct_id.help: Minimum percent identity for wfmash's mappings. Lower (for example 80, or 70 for genomes of different species of one genus) when the genomes are divergent, so distant ones still align; raise toward 95-98 for very close genomes (one species' strains or human haplotypes) to keep paralogues apart. Upstream's default 90 is the fallback.

wfmash_segment_length.help: wfmash segment length. Shorter (for example 1000-3000) for small or highly rearranged genomes such as bacteria or a single locus, so short homologous segments are found; longer (10000 or more) for large, repeat-rich eukaryotic genomes, to avoid spurious repeat alignments. Upstream's default 5000 is the fallback.

communities.help: true for large, many-chromosome genomes (eukaryotes): the genomes are split into communities (roughly one per chromosome) and a graph is built for each, then squeezed into one. Left unset (upstream's default, one graph for the whole set) for bacteria, organelles or a single locus.

vcf_spec.help: When the question asks for variants against one of the genomes, the PanSN prefix of that reference path (REF[:LEN], for example sample1#1), and vg deconstruct writes a VCF of the graph's variation relative to it. Left unset (upstream's default) no VCF is written.

multiqc_title.help: Title for the MultiQC report, when the user names the study.

pipeline.name: nf-core/pangenome
pipeline.core_rule: No samplesheet: --input is ONE bgzip-compressed FASTA holding every genome, sequence names in PanSN form (sample#haplotype#contig). Nessie writes a one-row sheet (sample, fasta) beside it only to record which A.ASM sample the file is; the submitter passes that row's path as --input. Combining several A.ASM samples' FASTAs into one is not supported yet, so the cohort must be exactly one sample whose file is already the combined FASTA.
pipeline.reference_requirement: No reference genome or database: the graph is built from the genomes in the input alone.

validation_rules: Exactly one sample: its file is the combined FASTA. Two or more A.ASM samples are refused until a combine step exists.
The FASTA must be bgzip-compressed (.fa.gz, .fna.gz or .fasta.gz); plain gzip fails samtools faidx inside the pipeline.
Sequence names must follow PanSN (sample#haplotype#contig), or vg deconstruct's output is wrong or missing.
n_haplotypes must equal the number of distinct sample#haplotype prefixes in the file.
notes: For a cohort of several genomes of one species or clade (bacterial strains, a crop's cultivars, phased human haplotypes) that someone has already combined into one PanSN-named FASTA. NExtSEEK holds no A.ASM samples yet. The step that would combine several A.ASM samples into one renamed, bgzipped FASTA (with n_haplotypes from the row count) is not built yet.

report_writer_guidance.purpose: Launch nf-core/pangenome on one A.ASM sample whose file is a combined, PanSN-named, bgzipped multi-genome FASTA.
report_writer_guidance.workflow_role: Selected when the user asks how several genomes of one species differ structurally, or for a pangenome or variation graph.
report_writer_guidance.output_expectation: A one-row sheet with header sample,fasta; --input is the fasta path.
population_priority: The one A.ASM sample holding the combined FASTA.
n_haplotypes from its GenomeCount, or ask.

runtime.basis: First guess from typical PGGB runs on one 16-CPU Luria node (Nessie's default submit); not measured on Luria. The one graph dominates: tens of bacterial genomes take about an hour, while large eukaryotic genomes can take days and need communities. Refine from real runs.
